Stamped
STAMPT
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Middle English stampen, to pound or crush with the foot, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: struck with the foot; impressed; crushed to powder. In Scripture the word belongs to two very different actions: the destruction of idols, and the trampling of a beast.

Biblical Definition

When Moses came down and dealt with the golden calf, he did not merely break it: I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it very small, even until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook (Deuteronomy 9:21). Notice how Moses names the object — your sin, not your idol — and notice the thoroughness, which is the point: burnt, stamped, ground, cast into water. Josiah does the same to the grove: burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people (2 Kings 23:6). Reformation in Scripture is never tidy or partial; the idol is reduced past the possibility of repair. The second use is terrible rather than righteous. Daniel’s fourth beast devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it (Daniel 7:7) — what it cannot eat it treads. And Ezekiel is told to make the sign with his own body: Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! (Ezekiel 6:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STAMP as to strike or beat forcibly with the bottom of the foot; to pound; to crush or bruise by beating; to impress with a mark; hence STAMPED, struck with the foot, impressed, crushed.

expand to see more

STAMP, v.t. — To strike or beat forcibly with the bottom of the foot, or by thrusting the foot downward.

To impress with some mark or figure; as, to stamp a coin.

To pound; to bray; to crush or bruise by beating; as, to stamp to powder.

STAMPED, pp. — Struck with the foot; impressed; coined; crushed.

Middle English stampen, of Germanic origin; connected with step and with the German stampfen.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 9:21 — "And I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it very small, even until it was as small as dust: and I cast the dust thereof into the brook that descended out of the mount."

2 Kings 23:6 — "And he brought out the grove from the house of the LORD, without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people."

Daniel 7:7 — "After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns."

Ezekiel 6:11 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence."

Modern Corruption

Moses grinds the calf to dust rather than reforming its use, which is the opposite of the modern instinct to baptize a corrupt practice by giving it a Christian meaning.

expand to see more

The golden calf was not offered to a foreign god. Aaron had proclaimed a feast to the LORD (Exodus 32:5), and the people were worshipping the God of Israel by an image of their own devising. That is precisely why Moses destroys it utterly rather than repurposing it. The second commandment forbids not only the worship of false gods but the worship of the true God by images and inventions He has not appointed, and the regulative principle of worship follows directly: what Scripture commands is required, and what Scripture has not commanded is not permitted in corporate worship. The recurring proposal to take a practice drawn from elsewhere and sanctify it by intention is the calf argument, and Deuteronomy 9:21 is the answer to it — burnt, stamped, ground to dust, and thrown in the brook.

Josiah’s reformation shows the same thoroughness carried into a nation’s public life, and it is worth noticing where he scattered the powder: upon the graves of the common people who had sacrificed there. Reformation in Scripture is not merely the addition of true worship but the removal of false, and it costs something. Daniel 7:7 supplies the sober counterweight. The beast that stamps the residue is a picture of a power that recognizes no such limits at all, and Daniel’s vision ends not with the beast’s success but with the Ancient of days seated and the judgment set. This dictionary reads Daniel as sixth-century prophecy from the prophet whose name it bears, against the standard critical redating that turns predictive prophecy into after-the-fact composition.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew daqaq (H1854), to crush or beat small; kathath (H3807), to beat or pound; raphas (H7429), to trample; Aramaic rephas (H7512), to stamp with the feet.

expand to see more

Hebrew daqaq (H1854) — to crush fine, to beat small; the calf ground as small as dust (Deuteronomy 9:21).

Hebrew kathath (H3807) — to beat or pound to pieces; used of Josiah’s purge (2 Kings 23:6).

Aramaic rephas (H7512) — to trample, to stamp; the fourth beast stamped the residue (Daniel 7:7).

Hebrew raqa (H7554) — to beat out, to stamp with the foot; Ezekiel’s prophetic sign (Ezekiel 6:11).

Hebrew asherah (H842) — the grove or wooden image Josiah burned and stamped to powder (2 Kings 23:6).

Usage

"I took your sin, the calf which ye had made... and stamped it (Deuteronomy 9:21) — Moses names the object your sin, and reduces it past repair."

"Stamped it small to powder (2 Kings 23:6) — reformation removes as well as adds, and it costs something."

"Stamped the residue with the feet of it (Daniel 7:7) — what the beast cannot devour, it treads."
